title: The clock that tamed time
text: Before mechanical clocks arrived, time was a matter of rough {{1}} (APPROXIMATE): the sun's position, the church bells, the rumbling of the stomach. The mechanical clock, perfected in Europe around the year 1300, changed that quietly and completely, cutting the day into twenty-four equal {{2}} (DIVIDE) that flowed regardless of sunrise or season. The consequences ran deep. Merchants could price a day's work; labourers found wages calculated at an {{3}} (HOUR) rate; and the monasteries that had built the first clocks to schedule prayer watched their invention slip its {{4}} (RELIGION) moorings and reorder secular life instead. Towns competed to raise the finest clock towers, whose {{5}} (REGULAR) reassured a population only just learning to live by minutes. Not everybody applauded. Writers grumbled that the new precision made existence feel {{6}} (HURRY) and artificial, ruled by a machine rather than by nature. The historian Lewis Mumford later argued that the clock, not the steam engine, was the key machine of the industrial age, because the habit of {{7}} (PUNCTUAL) had to exist before factories could demand it. Five centuries on, the timekeeper in your pocket outperforms every medieval astronomer, and most of us remain its obedient {{8}} (SERVE).
